La relation du Rôdeur avec la nature naît d'abord de l'expérience. Les animaux, les plantes, les saisons et les particularités du terrain font partie d'un environnement qu'il observe quotidiennement et dont dépend sa survie. Les connaissances acquises auprès de ses maîtres lui permettent de reconnaître les dangers naturels, de trouver les ressources nécessaires au voyage et de comprendre les comportements de nombreuses créatures.

Cette familiarité s'étend parfois à des savoirs plus anciens, transmis au sein des communautés ou par des maîtres versés dans les arts de la Théurgie. Le Rôdeur apprend alors à employer des pouvoirs qui renforcent son endurance, favorisent ses déplacements et approfondissent les relations qu'il entretient avec le monde vivant. Leur usage demeure étroitement associé aux activités qu'il pratique déjà : franchir un passage difficile, supporter les fatigues d'une longue marche, dissimuler sa présence ou retrouver un itinéraire oublié.

Les six disciplines traditionnelles de la profession reflètent cette orientation. Les Murs Intérieurs renforcent certaines résistances et capacités personnelles, tandis que les Voies du Mouvement soutiennent les déplacements dans les environnements difficiles. Les Masques de la Nature favorisent la dissimulation et l'adaptation à l'environnement. Les Appels de la Nature concernent les relations avec les animaux et certaines manifestations du monde naturel. La Voie de la Nature rassemble des pouvoirs utiles à la survie, et la Maîtrise des Sentiers développe les facultés nécessaires à la reconnaissance des pistes et des itinéraires.

La manière dont ces enseignements sont reçus dépend des traditions locales. Un Rôdeur du Nord peut conserver des connaissances transmises par sa famille ou acquises auprès d'un maître d'une grande ancienneté. Dans une communauté forestière, les savoirs liés aux animaux et aux plantes occuperont davantage de place. Certains personnages connaissent les rudiments de plusieurs disciplines, tandis que d'autres approfondissent un domaine particulier au fil de leur vie.

Les pouvoirs du Rôdeur prolongent ainsi son apprentissage plutôt qu'ils ne se substituent à lui. La magie lui apporte des moyens supplémentaires pour accomplir ses missions, mais sa valeur demeure fondée sur l'expérience du terrain, l'habileté aux armes et la capacité d'agir avec discernement.

Les liens et les devoirs

La réputation solitaire du Rôdeur dissimule souvent l'importance des relations qui structurent sa vie. Les patrouilles exigent une confiance profonde entre compagnons, et les longues absences rendent les retrouvailles particulièrement précieuses. Chez les Dúnedain du Nord, les familles conservent les traditions de leur peuple et maintiennent les liens entre des établissements éloignés les uns des autres. Dans l'Ithilien, les soldats partagent les dangers d'une guerre prolongée et les souvenirs d'un pays qu'ils ont vu progressivement abandonné.

Un Rôdeur connaît généralement plusieurs lieux où il sera accueilli. Il peut s'agir de la demeure d'un parent, d'une ferme isolée dont il a protégé les habitants ou d'un refuge connu de ses compagnons. Ces hospitalités comportent parfois des obligations réciproques : porter des nouvelles, rechercher un voyageur absent, réparer un passage endommagé ou avertir les habitants lorsque les traces d'un ennemi ont été découvertes.

Les relations avec les étrangers sont plus complexes. Dans certaines régions, les Rôdeurs inspirent de la gratitude et du respect ; ailleurs, leur apparence et leurs habitudes les rendent suspects. Leurs connaissances les conduisent à fréquenter des chemins dangereux et à poser des questions auxquelles les habitants ne savent pas toujours répondre. Un aubergiste de Bree peut préférer voir repartir rapidement un homme couvert de boue qui demande des nouvelles des voyageurs arrivés de l'est. Quelques jours plus tard, ce même homme aura peut-être empêché des pillards d'approcher du village.

La loyauté occupe une place importante dans leur existence. Elle s'adresse à un chef, à une communauté, à une terre ou à des compagnons dont ils ont appris à partager les dangers. Chez certains, cette fidélité s'étend au souvenir d'un royaume disparu ; chez d'autres, elle découle simplement de l'attachement à une vallée, à un village ou aux personnes qui y vivent.

Ces obligations peuvent entrer en conflit avec leurs aspirations personnelles. Les années de service éloignent parfois un Rôdeur de sa famille et rendent difficile toute existence stable. Un engagement ancien peut l'obliger à repartir alors qu'il espérait demeurer auprès des siens. À l'inverse, une rencontre imprévue ou une amitié nouvelle peut le conduire à remettre en question une mission dont il avait toujours accepté la nécessité.

Ces tensions donnent au personnage une profondeur particulière. Les choix qui lui sont imposés concernent souvent des personnes qu'il connaît, des lieux dont il garde le souvenir et des responsabilités qu'il a librement acceptées.

Le Rôdeur au fil des Âges

La place du Rôdeur dans la Terre du Milieu dépend profondément de l'époque choisie pour la campagne. La profession représente une tradition de surveillance et de connaissance des terres sauvages dont certaines formes existent bien avant l'apparition des Rôdeurs du Nord.

Au Premier Âge, il peut appartenir aux communautés humaines installées dans les forêts et les régions frontalières du Beleriand. Un chasseur du peuple de Haleth, établi dans la forêt de Brethil, connaît les chemins qui traversent les bois et participe à la défense de son territoire. Les gardiens elfes de Doriath ou des régions voisines possèdent également des compétences de surveillance, de déplacement et de combat adaptées à cette profession. Les guerres contre Morgoth rendent leurs connaissances précieuses pour protéger les habitations et suivre les mouvements de l'ennemi.

Au Deuxième Âge, le Rôdeur peut servir parmi les éclaireurs de peuples qui explorent ou défendent les terres situées entre les grands établissements humains. Les voyages des Númenóréens, les relations avec les populations de la Terre du Milieu et les conflits provoqués par l'expansion de Sauron offrent de nombreuses raisons d'entreprendre de longues expéditions. À la fin de l'Âge, la fondation d'Arnor et de Gondor donne naissance à de nouvelles frontières et à des réseaux de routes qu'il faut reconnaître, entretenir et protéger.

Au Troisième Âge, la profession connaît ses expressions les plus célèbres. Les Rôdeurs du Nord perpétuent l'héritage des Dúnedain après la destruction d'Arthedain, tandis que ceux de l'Ithilien défendent les anciennes terres du Gondor contre les serviteurs de Sauron. D'autres traditions existent parmi les chasseurs, les éclaireurs et les gardiens des communautés établies dans les régions sauvages du Rhovanion, des Montagnes Brumeuses ou des frontières méridionales.

Au Quatrième Âge, la chute de Sauron et la restauration du Royaume Réunifié ouvrent de nouvelles perspectives. Les anciens Rôdeurs du Nord peuvent reprendre ouvertement leur place au service d'un roi, tandis que les soldats de l'Ithilien participent à la sécurisation et au repeuplement de leur pays. De nouvelles routes sont rouvertes, des frontières réorganisées et des régions longtemps dangereuses redeviennent accessibles aux voyageurs. Les connaissances des Rôdeurs demeurent indispensables pour accompagner cette transformation.

Chaque époque influe ainsi sur les responsabilités du personnage. Un gardien du Premier Âge protège une communauté confrontée aux armées de Morgoth ; un éclaireur du Deuxième Âge découvre parfois des régions encore inconnues de son peuple. Le Rôdeur du Troisième Âge vit souvent dans un monde marqué par les pertes anciennes et la progression de l'Ombre, tandis que celui du Quatrième Âge participe à la restauration des terres pour lesquelles ses prédécesseurs ont combattu.

Prendre la route

Le départ d'un Rôdeur s'inscrit généralement dans la continuité de sa vocation. Une mission de surveillance peut le conduire au-delà de ses territoires habituels, tandis qu'un message urgent l'oblige à franchir des régions qu'il connaît seulement par les récits de ses maîtres. Les besoins d'une communauté, la disparition d'un compagnon ou la découverte de traces inquiétantes fournissent autant de raisons de prolonger un voyage.

Certains entreprennent une recherche plus personnelle. Un Rôdeur du Nord peut vouloir retrouver les vestiges d'un établissement disparu d'Arnor, éclaircir le sort d'un parent mort en patrouille ou rapporter un objet confié autrefois à la garde de sa famille. Un soldat de l'Ithilien cherche peut-être à rejoindre des proches réfugiés à l'ouest de l'Anduin ou à découvrir ce qu'est devenue une demeure abandonnée pendant les guerres.

Les voyages permettent également de rencontrer des peuples dont les coutumes diffèrent profondément des siennes. Un Dúnadan habitué aux chemins de l'Eriador devra apprendre à comprendre les usages des Béornides ou les exigences d'un voyage dans les montagnes. Un Rôdeur élevé dans les forêts de l'Ithilien découvrira d'autres formes de combat, d'autres manières de recevoir les étrangers et des traditions dont il ignorait jusqu'à l'existence.

Au sein d'une compagnie, son expérience devient rapidement précieuse. Il guide les voyageurs, examine les traces rencontrées sur la route et conseille ses compagnons lorsqu'ils doivent traverser une région dangereuse. Son entraînement martial lui permet de prendre part aux combats, mais aussi de préparer les déplacements et d'éviter des affrontements inutiles. La confiance qu'il inspire naît progressivement de la justesse de ses observations et de la constance de son comportement.

Les relations qui se forment au cours de ces expéditions peuvent modifier profondément sa manière de considérer ses obligations. Un Rôdeur ayant longtemps vécu parmi les siens découvre parfois des fidélités nouvelles, auxquelles il accorde autant de valeur qu'aux engagements hérités de sa famille. D'autres retrouvent dans leurs compagnons d'aventure une forme de solidarité semblable à celle qui unissait les patrouilles de leur jeunesse.

Le retour au pays possède alors une signification particulière. Après plusieurs années d'absence, les chemins familiers lui paraîtront peut-être inchangés, mais les communautés qu'il retrouve auront poursuivi leur histoire. Certains de ses proches auront disparu, de nouveaux dangers seront apparus et les responsabilités confiées à son départ auront évolué. Il devra trouver sa place dans un monde qu'il a contribué à protéger sans toujours pouvoir y demeurer.

Incarner un Rôdeur

Le Rôdeur offre la possibilité d'incarner un personnage dont les compétences reposent sur une expérience concrète du monde. Sa culture, son origine et les circonstances de sa formation déterminent cependant sa manière de vivre cette vocation.

Un jeune Dúnadan du Nord peut avoir grandi dans une famille attachée aux anciens serments d'Arnor, admirant les compagnons revenus de leurs patrouilles et désirant à son tour servir sous les ordres de son Chef. Un soldat de l'Ithilien peut porter le souvenir d'un domaine familial perdu, tandis qu'un chasseur des Hommes des Bois connaîtra surtout les nécessités de la vie dans une communauté exposée aux dangers des forêts. Ces origines donnent des significations différentes à des compétences pourtant semblables.

La relation du personnage avec ses maîtres, sa famille et ses compagnons constitue un élément essentiel de son histoire. Qui lui a enseigné les premiers chemins ? A-t-il déjà participé à une patrouille dont tous les membres ne sont pas revenus ? Existe-t-il une demeure où son retour est attendu, une frontière qu'il s'est engagé à défendre ou un ancien serment dont il connaît encore les paroles ?

Ses qualités peuvent s'accompagner de défauts liés à son expérience. Des années de surveillance rendent parfois un homme soupçonneux ; une succession de responsabilités difficiles peut l'amener à décider trop rapidement pour ses compagnons. D'autres Rôdeurs conservent une grande patience, un humour discret ou le goût des conversations prolongées lorsqu'ils retrouvent enfin la sécurité d'un foyer.

La profession convient particulièrement aux campagnes fondées sur les voyages, l'exploration des régions anciennes, la défense des communautés isolées et la lutte contre les serviteurs de l'Ombre. Elle prend également toute sa valeur dans les aventures où les personnages découvrent progressivement l'histoire des lieux qu'ils traversent.

Au-delà de ses compétences, le Rôdeur se définit par les responsabilités qu'il accepte et les liens qu'il entretient avec les terres qu'il parcourt. Ses voyages lui font découvrir de nouveaux peuples, éprouvent ses fidélités et l'amènent parfois à choisir entre plusieurs engagements également importants.

Note au Meneur — Le Rôdeur dans MERP-RMU

Le Rôdeur est une profession martiale et magique, fondée sur l'association des compétences de combat, de déplacement, de pistage et de survie avec des pouvoirs de Théurgie.

Dans MERP-RMU, ses caractéristiques primordiales sont la Constitution (Co) et l'Intuition (In). Il appartient aux semi-utilisateurs de Théurgie, conformément à l'identité traditionnelle de la profession.

Le Rôdeur dispose de six Listes de sorts de base :

ListeDomaine
Murs Intérieurs (Inner Walls)Résistance, endurance et renforcement de certaines capacités personnelles
Voies du Mouvement (Moving Ways)Déplacement et adaptation aux difficultés du terrain
Masques de la Nature (Nature's Guises)Camouflage, dissimulation et adaptation à l'environnement
Appels de la Nature (Nature's Summons)Relations avec les animaux et certaines manifestations naturelles
Voie de la Nature (Nature's Way)Survie et ressources nécessaires dans les terres sauvages
Maîtrise des Sentiers (Path Mastery)Reconnaissance des chemins, des pistes et des itinéraires

Les possibilités d'apprentissage et les effets précis de ces Listes restent ceux prévus par les mécanismes effectivement disponibles dans MERP-RMU.

Le Rôdeur possède une formation martiale étendue, adaptée à sa culture et aux missions qu'il exerce. L'arc constitue une arme particulièrement appropriée aux traditions de surveillance et de chasse, mais la profession n'impose aucune arme unique. Le choix de l'équipement et des protections doit correspondre à l'expérience du personnage, aux contraintes du terrain et aux règles RMU.

Une distinction essentielle concerne les Rôdeurs du Nord. Chez Tolkien, ils forment une communauté historique précise : les descendants des Dúnedain d'Arnor, placés sous l'autorité de leurs Chefs après la ruine du royaume. Les Rôdeurs de l'Ithilien appartiennent, quant à eux, aux forces du Gondor. La profession de Rôdeur dans MERP-RMU possède une portée plus large et représente également les chasseurs, les éclaireurs et les gardiens des terres sauvages issus d'autres peuples.

Le Meneur peut ainsi employer cette profession dans les différents Âges de la Terre du Milieu, en tenant compte de l'histoire des cultures concernées. Les Rôdeurs du Nord, en tant que communauté héritière d'Arnor, n'apparaissent qu'après la chute de l'Arthedain, tandis que les compétences représentées par la profession existent depuis des temps bien plus anciens.

Enfin, les six Listes magiques appartiennent au système de jeu. Les récits de Tolkien évoquent les connaissances exceptionnelles, les talents de guérison et les aptitudes remarquables de certains Rôdeurs, mais ne décrivent pas leur pratique selon une organisation en Listes de sorts. Cette adaptation permet d'intégrer leurs capacités à MERP-RMU tout en préservant leur identité littéraire.

Ranger

The Long Roads and the Guardianship of the Wild Lands

Night is drawing near on the East Road, a day's march from Bree. Since mid-afternoon a fine rain has fallen over the hills, soaking the tracks and filling the ditches along the ancient roadway. Three merchants' wagons struggle towards the first foothills of the Weather Hills. The horses are weary, and their drivers hope to reach a place where they can light a fire and pitch their shelters before darkness falls.

Some distance from the road, a man wrapped in a grey cloak watches their progress from a hilltop. His beard bears the marks of several days' travel, his boots are caked with mud, and a long sword hangs at his side. He studies the wagons, then turns towards a stand of stunted trees overlooking a narrow passage.

A few hours earlier he found the remains of a fire carefully concealed behind a bank. The damp earth still holds the footprints of several heavily shod men, together with the tracks of a creature whose gait he recognises. Among the ashes, a crudely forged arrowhead confirmed his suspicions: Orcs have come down from the mountains and are now prowling near the road.

The man crouches beside an outcrop of rock to study the ground. The slope descending towards the road is gentle enough for a swift attack, while the trees would offer the assailants an easy retreat. Farther north, an old path leads to a shallow ford. The merchants know nothing of it; perhaps their pursuers do not either.

The Ranger resumes his journey. He skirts the trees without a sound, identifies the tracks left by the Orcs, and determines that there are five of them, one wounded. They have spread out to watch the passage and are probably waiting for prey. Having marked their positions, he makes a circuit back to the road and reaches the wagons just as their drivers begin looking for a place to spend the night.

The merchant leading the convoy regards him with suspicion. The stranger appears poor, and his equipment has seen many years of service. Yet when he warns that the passage is dangerous and points out a safer way, there is something in his assurance that finally persuades the caravan-master to listen.

The wagons leave the road beneath the rain. The Ranger leads them to the ford, then sets off alone once the last wheels have crossed the stream. He still has to watch the road and make certain the Orcs have indeed left the neighbourhood.

In Bree, people may speak the following day of an unsettling wanderer seen near the Weather Hills. The merchants, however, will remember the man who spared them a dangerous encounter, without knowing his name or the reasons that drive him to roam these lands.

For years he has performed this duty in the service of those who still dwell in the ancient territories of the North. He is a Ranger, and the paths he protects cross the remnants of a kingdom whose very name has been forgotten by most of its inhabitants.

A Calling Born of the Frontiers

In Middle-earth, the wild lands stretch across immense spaces between kingdoms, towns, and inhabited countryside. Ancient roads pass through regions abandoned for generations. Stone bridges still span streams whose names have been lost, while ruined strongholds and villages bear witness to an age when these territories were more densely settled.

Communities established along these frontiers often rely on men and women able to range through such country, understand its resources, and recognise its dangers before they reach the dwellings of their people. Rangers fulfil that responsibility. Their knowledge encompasses hunting, tracking, travel over difficult terrain, the use of weapons, and survival far from settled lands. Some defend a particular frontier; others escort travellers, watch mountain passes, or seek out creatures threatening isolated communities.

Their calling takes different forms from one culture to another. In the North, the descendants of the Dúnedain of Arnor preserve a tradition of secretly watching over the former lands of their kingdom. In Gondor, the soldiers of Ithilien fight Sauron's servants in a country gradually deserted by its inhabitants. Elsewhere, a hunter of the Woodmen, a guardian of the valleys of Rhovanion, or an Elven scout may possess comparable experience gained in the service of their own people.

What first distinguishes a Ranger is the breadth of his skills. He can recognise a passable route, follow a trail, and determine whether a passage has recently been used. Changes in the weather, the habits of animals, and the nature of the ground provide him with essential information. Yet his duties also require him to understand people: merchants crossing a frontier, travellers who have lost their way, communities fearful of a new threat, and enemies attempting to pass through a territory unseen.

Such a life demands considerable endurance and sound judgement. In the remotest regions, decisions often have to be made without outside counsel. Misjudging the weather, attacking too soon, or imprudently choosing a path may endanger several companions. Experience teaches the Ranger to weigh these risks and retain enough strength and supplies to meet unforeseen difficulties.

Heirs of the Lost Kingdom

Among the Rangers of Middle-earth, those of the North hold a special place. They descend from the Dúnedain who survived the ruin of Arnor, the kingdom founded by Elendil at the end of the Second Age. After centuries of division and warfare against Angmar, Arthedain, the last kingdom of the northern Dúnedain, fell in the year 1974 of the Third Age. The survivors preserved their lineage, their traditions, and the memory of their kings, but ceased openly to exercise their former authority.

Aranarth, son of the last king Arvedui, became the first Chieftain of the Dúnedain of the North. Under his leadership and that of his successors, the descendants of Isildur continued to dwell in the remote parts of Eriador. Some remained with their families in secluded settlements, while others patrolled the borders of the lands that were still inhabited. Their fidelity to the inheritance of the past endured in part through their ties with the Elves of Rivendell, where the heirs of their line were raised and educated.

The Rangers of the North keep watch over a country that has largely forgotten their history. The people of Bree know these men with their worn cloaks, stern faces, and long swords, yet have little understanding of their origins or their missions. The Hobbits of the Shire likewise live under their protection, most of them unaware of how many dangers are turned back beyond their borders.

This duty requires a loyalty difficult to explain to those who do not share its causes. Rangers patrol the ancient roads, watch the routes taken by Orcs and wolves, seek missing travellers, and maintain contact between scattered communities. Their knowledge of Arnor's ruins, abandoned fortifications, and old lines of communication allows them to move through regions where strangers readily lose their way.

Their humble appearance sometimes conceals a remarkable education. Some know the ancient languages, the tales of their forebears, and the history of the wars that have shaken Eriador. Such learning is passed down within families and through teachers devoted to the preservation of their people. Training in arms, knowledge of the land, and the arts of war complete an education intended to keep alive a royal tradition that has become almost invisible.

Aragorn, son of Arathorn, embodies this inheritance at the close of the Third Age. Known as Strider, he spends many years travelling through the North and other regions of Middle-earth. His life illustrates the range of talents that the most accomplished Rangers may possess: exceptional endurance, knowledge of peoples, mastery of weapons, skill in leadership, and healing lore inherited from ancient traditions.

Nevertheless, every Ranger of the North has a life of his own. Not all descend from the line of the Chieftains, nor do all share the same duties. Some live among their loved ones, take part in their community's decisions, and enjoy the ordinary pleasures of family life. Their long absences, the wounds they bring home from patrols, and the loss of companions nevertheless recall the price at which their people have maintained their freedom.

The Guardians of Ithilien

In the South, the Rangers of Ithilien belong to a different tradition. Their country lies between the Anduin and the mountains overlooking Mordor. Once prosperous, it has gardens, orchards, and towns whose remains can still be seen amid the vegetation. Yet the advance of the Shadow and attacks from the east have gradually forced its inhabitants to abandon their homes.

The Rangers of Gondor have known these lands since childhood or have been trained to defend them. They move in small bands, conceal themselves in the woods, and watch the paths used by enemy troops. Their equipment favours mobility: clothing in shades of green and brown, bows, swords, and protection suited to long marches. Their operations involve observing enemy movements, passing on intelligence, laying ambushes, and disrupting the enemy's passage.

Under the command of Faramir, son of Denethor, these men continue to defend a territory that Gondor can no longer occupy permanently. The hidden refuge of Henneth Annûn allows them to assemble, tend their wounded, and plan their expeditions out of sight. Men such as Mablung and Damrod exemplify their experience and the discipline required by a war fought far from the kingdom's great fortresses.

The daily life of these soldiers differs from that of the guardians of the North. Their mission belongs to a military organisation, with officers, orders, and coordinated operations. At times they receive support from their countrymen west of the Anduin, but must act swiftly when they cross the river and enter threatened lands.

Their attachment to Ithilien nevertheless gives their struggle a deeply personal meaning. Deserted houses, old walls overgrown with plants, and orchards returned to the wild recall what their families have lost. Recognising an ancient path, uncovering a well buried beneath the grass, or glimpsing the remains of a home once known to their parents may revive the memory of the country they hope one day to reclaim.

The traditions of the North and Gondor thus reveal two ways of fulfilling a Ranger's calling. In both, martial courage rests upon an intimate knowledge of the country, maintained through long years of vigilance and fighting. Yet their allegiances, obligations, and available means remain profoundly different.

Learning the Ways of the Wild

A Ranger's training generally begins long before he is capable of covering great distances alone. Among the Dúnedain of the North, young people gradually accompany their elders along hunting trails, forest paths, and the routes connecting their settlements. In Ithilien, recruits learn from experienced soldiers to recognise tracks, use natural cover, and move without betraying their group's position. Elsewhere, instruction follows the customs of each community.

The early years are devoted to the knowledge necessary for daily life. The apprentice learns to maintain his equipment, kindle a fire in the rain, find drinkable water, and choose shelter sufficiently protected from the wind. Observing the seasons teaches him which paths remain open in winter, where rivers become dangerous after heavy rain, and how vegetation changes a region's appearance throughout the year.

Tracking demands particular attention. A footprint in the mud reveals the passage of a man or an animal, but its interpretation depends on the ground and the circumstances. The Ranger learns to compare several signs: the depth and arrangement of the marks, displaced branches, freshly disturbed soil, and abandoned debris. As his experience grows, he becomes able to reconstruct a group's movements, judge its pace, and sometimes discover where it halted.

Knowledge of the country extends beyond reading tracks. Ancient roads, hunting paths, and hidden fords form a geography preserved through instruction and practice. Place-names often retain the memory of old dangers, difficult passages, or vanished communities. A Ranger who knows a region's history may understand why a road was deserted or why certain families still avoid a particular valley.

Training in weapons complements these lessons. Skill with the bow is especially valuable for hunting, watching, and fighting at a distance, but the sword, spear, axe, or knife also has its place according to local traditions. The young Ranger practises fighting in confined spaces, defending a wounded companion, and withdrawing in good order when the enemy holds the advantage.

His teachers place particular emphasis on judgement. In dangerous country, discovering an enemy trail does not necessarily mean it should be followed at once. The Ranger must consider his mission, his strength, and the risks faced by those with him. This discipline gradually distinguishes the apprentice from a merely skilled hunter: his knowledge becomes the instrument of a wider responsibility.

Life upon the Roads

Long marches occupy much of a Ranger's life. Some regularly traverse the territory whose passages they watch; others set out on expeditions lasting several weeks to carry a message, scout a region, or accompany travellers.

Preparing for departure demands particular care. Equipment must be light enough for rapid travel while still providing the means to withstand cold, rain, and several nights far from habitation. The Ranger chooses clothing suited to the climate, protects his food from damp, and keeps his weapons in good condition. His pack often contains a few simple tools whose value becomes apparent along the way: a whetstone, strong thread, leather-repair implements, cord, and small vessels for carrying water or remedies.

Food depends as much upon provisions carried as upon the resources found along the road. Hunting and gathering may sometimes lighten the burden, but a good traveller also knows when game grows scarce and which regions may require several days' march without a spring. Unknown country calls for greater caution, particularly when a sizeable company must be fed.

The nights demand equal vigilance. Choosing a campsite involves assessing the ground, possible approaches, and the presence of animals or enemies. A fire provides warmth and comfort, but its smoke and light may reveal the group's position. The Ranger therefore seeks to adapt his companions' habits to the circumstances, even if he must ask them to endure a few hours of discomfort for their safety.

Such a life develops a profound familiarity with the landscapes crossed. The succession of ridges, the arrangement of streams, and changes in vegetation allow him to find his way even when paths vanish. He also learns to recognise signs of human presence: freshly cut wood, the remains of a hearth, a hunting trap, or traces of an old working.

Long experience in the wild also brings a very practical knowledge of one's own limitations. Poorly tended wounds, privation, and years spent sleeping on cold ground leave lasting marks. Even the hardiest Rangers need rest, care, and places where they can regain their strength. The hospitality received during their travels therefore becomes precious, and some encounters grow into friendships lasting many years.

Keeping Watch and Fighting

Combat forms part of the Ranger's duties, though the circumstances in which it arises often differ from a clash between armies. In isolated regions, an enemy band is rarely encountered on favourable ground. Orcs use narrow passes, woods, and ruins to lay ambushes; brigands seek to surprise travellers where help is distant. Knowledge of the terrain then becomes as important as skill at arms.

When time permits, the Ranger seeks to discover his adversaries' positions and intentions. The number of tracks, the presence of horses, the remains of a camp, or the direction of patrols offers a first indication of the forces he may face. Such preparation allows him to choose a safe passage, warn allies, or position his companions before an engagement.

Rangers of the northern regions must often act in small groups with limited resources. The soldiers of Ithilien have perfected ambush warfare against forces crossing their territory. Elsewhere, defending an isolated village or mountain pass calls for different methods. Experience teaches each Ranger to make use of his companions' strengths and the advantages offered by the ground.

Stealth plays a major part in such operations. Approaching an enemy unseen, remaining motionless during a watch, or crossing exposed ground may be the best way to avoid a deadly confrontation. Such caution comes from training and a precise understanding of what the surroundings make possible.

When battle becomes inevitable, the Ranger remains a formidable opponent. Years of travel have strengthened his endurance, and the encounters of his patrols have taught him to remain mobile. He also knows how to weigh the consequences of a wound, recognise when retreat has become necessary, and protect those who depend upon him.

Victory often has a modest but essential meaning: a convoy reaches its destination, a family returns to its home, or a passage remains safe for a few more weeks. Where the authority of kingdoms reaches only with difficulty, these repeated successes allow communities to continue their lives.

Nature and the Ranger's Powers

A Ranger's relationship with nature arises first from experience. Animals, plants, seasons, and the features of the terrain belong to surroundings he observes every day and upon which his survival depends. The knowledge acquired from his teachers enables him to recognise natural dangers, find the resources needed for travel, and understand the behaviour of many creatures.

This familiarity sometimes extends to more ancient lore, passed down within communities or by masters versed in the arts of Channeling. The Ranger then learns to wield powers that strengthen his endurance, aid his movements, and deepen his relationship with the living world. Their use remains closely connected to activities he already practises: crossing difficult ground, enduring the weariness of a long march, concealing his presence, or recovering a forgotten route.

The profession's six traditional disciplines reflect this purpose. Inner Walls strengthen certain resistances and personal abilities, while Moving Ways aid movement through difficult environments. Nature's Guises favour concealment and adaptation to the surroundings. Nature's Summons concern relations with animals and certain manifestations of the natural world. Nature's Way gathers powers useful for survival, and Path Mastery develops the faculties needed to recognise tracks and routes.

The manner in which these teachings are received depends upon local traditions. A Ranger of the North may preserve knowledge handed down within his family or acquired from a master of great age. In a forest community, lore concerning animals and plants may receive greater emphasis. Some characters learn the rudiments of several disciplines, while others devote themselves to mastering a particular field over the course of their lives.

The Ranger's powers thus extend his training rather than take its place. Magic grants him further means to fulfil his missions, but his worth remains grounded in experience of the land, skill at arms, and the ability to act with discernment.

Bonds and Duties

The Ranger's solitary reputation often conceals the importance of the relationships that shape his life. Patrols demand deep trust between companions, and long absences make reunions especially precious. Among the Dúnedain of the North, families preserve the traditions of their people and maintain ties between settlements far apart. In Ithilien, soldiers share the perils of a prolonged war and the memories of a country they have seen gradually deserted.

A Ranger generally knows several places where he will be welcomed. They may include a relative's home, an isolated farm whose inhabitants he has protected, or a refuge familiar to his companions. Such hospitality sometimes carries obligations on both sides: bringing news, searching for a missing traveller, repairing a damaged crossing, or warning the inhabitants when traces of an enemy have been discovered.

Relations with strangers are more complicated. In some regions, Rangers inspire gratitude and respect; elsewhere, their appearance and habits make them objects of suspicion. Their knowledge leads them along dangerous paths and prompts them to ask questions that the inhabitants cannot always answer. An innkeeper in Bree may prefer to see a mud-covered man depart quickly after he has asked for news of travellers from the east. A few days later, that same man may have prevented raiders from approaching the village.

Loyalty holds an important place in their lives. It may be owed to a leader, a community, a country, or companions with whom they have learned to share danger. For some, this fidelity extends to the memory of a vanished kingdom; for others, it arises simply from attachment to a valley, a village, or the people who live there.

Such duties may conflict with personal hopes. Years of service sometimes keep a Ranger far from his family and make a settled life difficult. An old commitment may compel him to depart again when he had hoped to remain among his own. Conversely, an unexpected encounter or a new friendship may lead him to question a mission whose necessity he had always accepted.

These tensions give the character particular depth. The choices he faces often concern people he knows, places he remembers, and responsibilities he has freely undertaken.

The Ranger Through the Ages

The Ranger's place in Middle-earth depends profoundly on the period chosen for the campaign. The profession represents a tradition of vigilance and knowledge of the wild whose forms existed long before the emergence of the Rangers of the North.

In the First Age, he may belong to human communities established in the forests and borderlands of Beleriand. A hunter of the people of Haleth, dwelling in the Forest of Brethil, knows the paths through the woods and helps defend his land. Elven guardians of Doriath or neighbouring regions likewise possess skills in watchfulness, travel, and fighting that suit this profession. The wars against Morgoth make their knowledge precious for protecting settlements and following enemy movements.

In the Second Age, the Ranger may serve among the scouts of peoples exploring or defending lands between great settlements of Men. The voyages of the Númenóreans, their relations with the inhabitants of Middle-earth, and the conflicts caused by Sauron's expansion provide many reasons to undertake long expeditions. At the end of the Age, the founding of Arnor and Gondor brings new frontiers and networks of roads that must be surveyed, maintained, and protected.

In the Third Age, the profession takes its most celebrated forms. The Rangers of the North carry on the inheritance of the Dúnedain after the fall of Arthedain, while the Rangers of Ithilien defend Gondor's ancient lands against Sauron's servants. Other traditions exist among the hunters, scouts, and guardians of communities established in the wild regions of Rhovanion, the Misty Mountains, and the southern frontiers.

In the Fourth Age, Sauron's downfall and the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom open new prospects. The former Rangers of the North may openly take their place once more in the service of a king, while the soldiers of Ithilien help secure and resettle their country. Ancient roads are reopened, frontiers reorganised, and regions long beset by danger become accessible to travellers once again. Rangers' knowledge remains indispensable in guiding this transformation.

Each age thus shapes the character's duties. A guardian of the First Age protects a community facing Morgoth's armies; a scout of the Second Age may discover regions still unknown to his people. The Ranger of the Third Age often lives in a world marked by ancient losses and the advance of the Shadow, while his successor in the Fourth Age helps restore the lands for which his forebears fought.

Taking to the Road

A Ranger's departure generally follows naturally from his calling. A mission of vigilance may lead him beyond his customary territory, while an urgent message compels him to cross regions he knows only from his teachers' accounts. A community's needs, a missing companion, or the discovery of troubling tracks offer as many reasons for extending a journey.

Some undertake a more personal quest. A Ranger of the North may wish to recover the remains of a vanished settlement of Arnor, learn the fate of a relative killed on patrol, or return an object once entrusted to his family's keeping. A soldier of Ithilien may seek relatives who took refuge west of the Anduin or try to discover what became of a home abandoned during the wars.

Journeys also bring encounters with peoples whose customs differ profoundly from his own. A Dúnadan accustomed to the roads of Eriador must learn the ways of the Beornings or the demands of travel through the mountains. A Ranger raised in the forests of Ithilien will discover other forms of combat, other customs of hospitality, and traditions of whose existence he had been entirely unaware.

Within a company, his experience soon proves invaluable. He guides the travellers, examines tracks encountered along the road, and advises his companions when they must cross dangerous country. His martial training enables him to fight, but also to prepare their movements and avoid needless confrontations. The trust he inspires grows gradually from the soundness of his observations and the constancy of his conduct.

The relationships formed during these expeditions may profoundly alter his understanding of his obligations. A Ranger who has long lived among his own discovers new loyalties, sometimes valuing them as highly as the commitments inherited from his family. Others find in their fellow adventurers a solidarity resembling that which united the patrols of their youth.

The return home then acquires particular significance. After several years away, familiar paths may seem unchanged, yet the communities he revisits have continued their lives. Some of his loved ones will have died, new dangers will have arisen, and the duties entrusted to him when he left will have changed. He must find his place in a world he has helped protect without always being able to remain within it.

Playing a Ranger

The Ranger offers an opportunity to portray a character whose abilities are founded upon direct experience of the world. His culture, origins, and the circumstances of his training nevertheless determine how he lives out this calling.

A young Dúnadan of the North may have grown up in a family devoted to Arnor's ancient oaths, admiring the companions who returned from patrol and longing to serve in turn under the orders of his Chieftain. A soldier of Ithilien may carry the memory of a lost family estate, while a hunter of the Woodmen will know above all the demands of life in a community exposed to the dangers of the forests. These origins give different meanings to otherwise similar skills.

The character's relationship with his teachers, family, and companions is an essential part of his history. Who taught him the first paths? Has he ever joined a patrol from which some members did not return? Is there a home where his return is awaited, a frontier he has sworn to defend, or an ancient oath whose words he still remembers?

His strengths may be accompanied by weaknesses rooted in experience. Years of vigilance sometimes make a man suspicious; a succession of difficult responsibilities may lead him to make decisions too hastily on behalf of his companions. Other Rangers retain great patience, a quiet sense of humour, or a liking for long conversations when at last they find the safety of a hearth.

The profession is particularly well suited to campaigns centred on travel, exploration of ancient lands, the defence of isolated communities, and the struggle against the servants of the Shadow. It also comes into its own in adventures where characters gradually uncover the history of the places they cross.

Beyond his skills, the Ranger is defined by the responsibilities he accepts and the bonds he maintains with the lands through which he travels. His journeys bring him among new peoples, test his loyalties, and sometimes force him to choose between commitments of equal importance.

Game Master's Note — The Ranger in MERP-RMU

The Ranger is a martial and magical profession, combining skills in combat, movement, tracking, and survival with powers of Channeling.

In MERP-RMU, his Prime Stats are Constitution (Co) and Intuition (In). He is a semi-spell-user of Channeling, in keeping with the profession's traditional identity.

The Ranger has six Base Spell Lists:

Spell ListDomain
Inner WallsResistance, endurance, and the strengthening of certain personal abilities
Moving WaysMovement and adaptation to difficult terrain
Nature's GuisesCamouflage, concealment, and adaptation to the surroundings
Nature's SummonsRelations with animals and certain manifestations of the natural world
Nature's WaySurvival and the resources needed in the wild lands
Path MasteryRecognition of paths, tracks, and routes

The opportunities to learn these Lists, their precise effects, and their limitations remain those provided by the mechanics actually available in MERP-RMU.

The Ranger receives extensive martial training suited to his culture and the missions he undertakes. The bow is especially appropriate to traditions of surveillance and hunting, but the profession requires no single weapon. The choice of equipment and armour must reflect the character's experience, the demands of the terrain, and the RMU rules.

An essential distinction concerns the Rangers of the North. In Tolkien's writings, they form a specific historical community: the descendants of the Dúnedain of Arnor, led by their Chieftains after the kingdom's fall. The Rangers of Ithilien, by contrast, belong to the forces of Gondor. The Ranger profession in MERP-RMU has a broader scope and also represents hunters, scouts, and guardians of the wild drawn from other peoples.

The Game Master may therefore use this profession in the different Ages of Middle-earth, taking account of the history of the cultures concerned. The Rangers of the North, as a community inheriting the legacy of Arnor, emerge only after the fall of Arthedain, whereas the skills represented by the profession have existed since far more ancient times.

Finally, the six magical Lists belong to the game system. Tolkien's stories describe the exceptional knowledge, healing abilities, and remarkable talents of certain Rangers, but do not present their practice as an arrangement of Spell Lists. This adaptation integrates their abilities into MERP-RMU while preserving their literary identity.
